newsitem.title: USA: Mystery disease is killing off alligators.
newsitem.headline: Mystery disease is killing off alligators.

text.p: Dozens of captive alligators have died in Florida in recent months from a mystery disease that researchers said Thursday could threaten their estimated 1.5 million counterparts in the wild.

"We thought alligators were incredibly resilient animals, with surprisingly few cases of disease," Kent Vliet, a University of Florida alligator expert and member of a team of researchers studying the problem, said. "We were wrong."

Beginning in fall 1995, large male alligators in one enclosure at the St. Augustine Alligator Farm and Zoological Park suddenly began getting sick and dying at the rate of about a half dozen per day. All told, about 77 out of 89 alligators in the first enclosure died, among them some that were more than 60 years old, up to 12 feet (4 meters) and weighed as much as 800 pounds (360 kg).
The disease also spread to another enclosure of 160 alligators, both male and female.

Wildlife veterinarians performed necropsies, animal versions of autopsies, and found the animals had been infected with a new strain of mycoplasma bacteria, which can cause arthritis and pneumonia in humans and animals.

The bacteria also has been blamed for upper respiratory infections in the endangered desert tortoise of the American Southwest and the Florida gopher tortoise. The source of the bacteria was not immediately known.

Once infected, the alligators become extremely sluggish and stop moving. Vliet said research indicated that mycoplasma infection compromises the alligators' immune systems, allowing other secondary bacterial or viral invaders to overwhelm and kill them.
To treat the alligators, Vliet's team has begun treating them with regular antibiotic injections, but he said it was too early to tell whether the treatment would be effective.
